title: Armadillo-Inspired Robot Curls Into a Ball to Protect Fragile Cargo
summary:
The three-banded armadillo has a superpower: when threatened, it rolls into a nearly impenetrable ball. Now engineers have built a robot that does the same thing to protect fragile electronics.

"Like an armadillo, the new device changes shape to protect itself with a rigid shell," says study leader Jianyu Zhou, a mechanical engineer at North Carolina State University. The team describes its morphing robot in the May 27 issue of Science Advances.

The robot starts out flat. When a sensor detects a vibration — even a gentle touch — it sends a signal to an actuator. That turns on a tiny heater, warming a muscle-like material. One layer expands while another contracts, pulling the device into a wheel-like shape. The whole process takes about a minute. A hard, 3-D printed outer shell guards the contents from puncture, breakage, or falls. There is also an inner space that can hold a small payload.

It took the engineers more than a year to create the robot. The challenge was finding a design that could curl up and lock into itself. They used a layered approach: a hard outer shell with bendable plates, flexible inner layers that act like synthetic muscles, and an inner skeleton of almost-triangular pieces that lock together. Zhou says it comes together like an origami creation.

The work comes from the lab of Yong Zhu, which focuses on flexible electronics and soft robots. Inspired by caterpillars, these squishy robots might one day wriggle through debris after a natural disaster to search for survivors or explore hazardous sites like the deep ocean floor or active volcanoes. But such outings could crush or fry them. "The natural question," Zhu says, was "how to protect those."

Nina Attias, a conservation biologist who studies armadillos, is not surprised by the inspiration. "Once you start knowing about them, you see that these are pretty amazing creatures," she says. Only three of the 20 known armadillo species can roll into a ball, and they are super-sensitive to vibrations.

Why does this matter? Soft robots could go places humans cannot, but they need armor to survive. This armadillo-inspired shell might be the answer.
why_it_matters: Soft robots are being designed for places people cannot safely go — searching rubble after an earthquake or mapping the ocean floor — but a squishy machine is easy to puncture or fry, so this armadillo-style shell shows how nature-inspired robots could become tough enough to be genuinely useful rather than just clever.

background_read: Science Advances (an online research journal published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the group behind the journal Science) printed the study in its May 27 issue. The work comes from the lab of Yong Zhu at North Carolina State University (a large public research university in the U.S. state of North Carolina), which builds flexible electronics and soft robots.

Soft robots are a young field: instead of stiff motors and metal joints, they use air, heat or chemical reactions to bend and squeeze, which makes them good at handling delicate objects or crawling into tight spaces. The trade-off is that a squishy machine is easy to puncture, crush or fry.

Engineers copy nature all the time — an approach called biomimicry. Velcro came from plant burrs, fast-train noses were shaped after kingfisher beaks, and swimming suits were modelled on shark skin. Armadillos are the natural next model for armour.

NASA has used origami crease patterns, such as the Miura fold, to pack large solar panels tightly for launch and unfold them once in space — roughly the same folding problem this robot team had to solve.

Only a few of the roughly 20 known armadillo species can roll into a ball, and Nina Attias, a conservation biologist who studies them, notes that they are extremely sensitive to vibrations — the same signal the robot uses to know when to protect itself.

perspectives.description: For robotics labs this is a neat solution to a real problem: a robot that carries its own protective armour can be sent into rubble, the deep ocean or a volcano without being destroyed on contact. It also shows that a fold-up shell can be built from cheap 3-D printed parts and layered materials.

Sceptics note that curling up in about a minute is slow, and that the robot has so far only been shown locking into a ball, not crawling through a collapsed building or surviving real heat and pressure. Turning a lab demo into a tool that saves lives usually takes many more years.

Borrowing designs from animals has a long record: Velcro from burrs, train noses from kingfisher beaks, swimsuits from shark skin. Armadillos are simply a good answer to a very old engineering question — how to carry something fragile through a dangerous place.

If the shell can be scaled up and made cheaper, the same folding trick could protect drones, medical devices or space equipment. Biologists also gain something: headlines about robot armadillos remind people that these animals exist and are under pressure from habitat loss.
